summary: An exact translative-tiling example with 30 golden rhombi and every zone of 10 faces would answer Grünbaum's open question for k = 10, where he says 'No information is available for any k >= 10.' It would be the first case beyond the doubly indented icosahedra D1, D2 (k = 8). This is a natural research note for discrete geometers and crystallographers studying non-convex parallelohedra, a live topic (Senechal and Taylor, Acta Cryst. A 2023). Open-problem wording verified (the PDF text renders >= as 'C'). The same page says 'None of the other isozonohedra obtainable by indentation of F or T seems to be a parallelohedron', which is informal evidence against indentations of the triacontahedron T. An example would need to go beyond those, or overturn that impression, and the account should mention the remark.

Six edge directions, with each pair spanning one golden rhombus that occurs twice, give 15*2 = 30 faces and 10 faces per zone. The convex triacontahedron has exactly these face and zone data but is not a parallelohedron, since convex parallelohedra have zones of 4 or 6. Six equiangular lines in R^3 are unique up to isometry, so this is the natural congruent-rhombus class for k = 10. Still, the question allows other configurations, for example zones that revisit directions or more than 30 faces.
G1 and G2 contradict each other: G1 asserts existence in the class where G2 asserts non-existence. They are alternative outcomes of one search, not joint claims.

summary: A finite exhaustive search showing that no 30-face golden-rhombus polyhedron on the six icosahedral directions, with every zone of 10 faces, is a parallelohedron would confirm Grünbaum's informal remark about triacontahedron indentations. It would not settle his question for k = 10: rhombic monohedra with zones of 10 faces need not have exactly 30 faces or use each direction pair once. As a stand-alone negative result in a restricted class, it would fit as a section of a paper rather than a paper of its own. Paper-worthiness has not been shown. The paraphrased definition also leaves out one of Grünbaum's conditions.

findings.message: Research interest is not established. To clear the bar, extend it to a class that decides k = 10, or combine it with a positive construction or a structural obstruction that explains the search result.

summary: Classifying every pyramid over a square base, apex anywhere, that tiles space would settle the quadrilateral-pyramid part of Goldberg's question on the space-filling pentahedra for square bases. It needs Dehn-invariant vanishing across a three-parameter family, which goes well beyond Duval's one-parameter Galois-theoretic theorem. The audience is discrete geometers in tiling and scissors congruence. The account understates prior partial results: Duval's paper also settles slices beyond the right square pyramids.

findings.message: Omitted partial result within P1's scope. Duval derives from Theorem 1 that the symmetric halvings T2(h) and T4(h) of the right square pyramid have trivial Dehn invariant only at h = 1/sqrt2. T4(h) is the square pyramid with apex above a base vertex, and its only zero-Dehn member is the classical one-third-cube pyramid. T2(h) is a rectangle-based pyramid with apex above an edge midpoint. The candidate says only that the right square pyramids are settled. The account should list every slice already decided, so a reader can see what is new.
